samples.text:
In many big cities, the price of houses and flats is very high, and workers like nurses and teachers cannot afford to live close to where they work. This situation causes several problems, and in this essay I will discuss them and suggest some solutions.

The first problem is that these workers have to travel very long distances every day. For example, a nurse who lives outside the city may need to spend two hours in a train to arrive to the hospital. This make them very tired and stressed, and a tired nurse or teacher cannot do their job well. Another problem is that many of them decide to leave their job or move to a cheaper city. As a result, hospitals and schools in the city do not have enough staffs, and people who live there receive worse service. For instance, classes become bigger and patients must wait longer for treatment.

There are some solutions to this problem. Firstly, the government can build special houses for essential workers with lower rent. This is already happening in some countries and it help workers to stay near their workplace. Secondly, employers such as hospitals could give their staff extra money for housing or for transport. Thirdly, the government should control the rent prices, so the landlords cannot increase them too much every year.

In conclusion, the high cost of housing in cities make it difficult for essential workers to live near their job, which cause tiredness and a shortage of staff. I think the best solution is to build affordable housing for these workers and also give them some financial support.
samples.why: Both parts covered with relevant points · solutions listed rather than developed · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly) · adequate vocabulary · repeated subject-verb agreement and preposition errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In many major cities, property prices and rents have risen so steeply that key workers such as nurses, teachers and police officers are being priced out of the areas they serve. This trend has serious consequences for both the workers themselves and the wider community, although there are several ways in which it could be addressed.

For individual workers, the main problem is the burden of long commutes. Many essential staff are forced to live in distant suburbs or neighbouring towns, which means spending several hours travelling each day, often on shifts that start early in the morning or finish late at night. This leads to exhaustion and stress, and it is not surprising that many eventually decide to leave the profession or relocate to cheaper regions. The consequences for the city are equally serious. Hospitals and schools struggle to recruit and keep staff, resulting in larger classes, longer waiting times and a greater dependence on expensive temporary workers.

One effective solution would be for local governments to build or subsidise housing reserved specifically for essential workers, offered at rents linked to their salaries rather than to the market. Public employers could also play a role, for example by converting unused land owned by hospitals into staff accommodation. In addition, a housing allowance for those working in high-cost areas would help to close the gap between wages and living expenses. In the longer term, governments need to increase the overall supply of affordable homes, since the underlying problem is that there are simply not enough housing for ordinary earners.

In conclusion, unaffordable housing leaves essential workers exhausted and cities short of vital staff. Dedicated affordable housing, targeted allowances and a broader increase in housing supply would together help to keep these workers close to where they are needed.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · problems for workers and the city extended and supported · logical progression with varied linking · good collocations (priced out, underlying problem) · frequent error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The soaring cost of urban housing has created a paradox in many cities: the people whose work keeps them functioning, including nurses, teachers and care staff, increasingly cannot afford to live in them. This essay argues that the problem damages both the wellbeing of these workers and the quality of public services, and that it calls for targeted housing policy alongside broader reform.

At a personal level, being priced out imposes a heavy daily toll. Essential workers displaced to distant towns face lengthy commutes that, combined with irregular shifts, leave little time for rest or family life. Chronic fatigue is not merely unpleasant; in professions where alertness matters, such as nursing, it can compromise the safety of those in their care. Unsurprisingly, many eventually conclude that the sacrifice is not worth it and either leave the profession or move to cheaper regions. For the city, the cumulative effect is a persistent shortage of skilled staff. Schools rely on a rotating cast of supply teachers, hospitals spend heavily on agency nurses, and residents experience longer waits and less continuity of care. Emergency services, too, become less resilient when those who staff them live an hour or more away.

The most direct response is to provide housing designated for key workers, with rents set as a proportion of income rather than market value. Public bodies are often well placed to do this, since hospitals, universities and councils frequently own land that could be developed for staff accommodation. Location-based salary supplements can offer further relief, although they risk being absorbed by rising rents if supply remains constrained. Ultimately, therefore, such measures must be accompanied by a sustained expansion of affordable housing, achieved through planning reform and public construction.

In conclusion, unaffordable housing exhausts essential workers and weakens the services cities depend on. Dedicated key-worker housing offers immediate relief, but lasting improvement depends on building enough homes for ordinary earners.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses both parts with extended, well-supported ideas · solutions evaluated, not just listed · cohesion managed skilfully · precise, natural vocabulary (imposes a heavy toll, continuity of care) · wide range of accurate structures.
